title: Cue Catalog Fugue — notes and micro-experiments
content_body:
Context / intent:
This is a personal scratchpad for building a small, curated catalog of cue-forms (short instruction fragments) and how they interact when layered. Goal is pragmatic: collect compact examples that reveal brittle interactions (cue drift, tokenization split, style bleed) and assemble a canonical small few-shot set we can ship into the prompt library as a lightweight regression harness.

Notes style: messy; indexable by search terms. Use this to reproduce quickly for evals and for adding variants to the template repo.

High-level taxonomy (working):
- Anchor cues: clear role + format (e.g., "You are a friendly assistant: respond in 3 bullets")
- Micro-primers: single-sentence prefatory statements (e.g., "If uncertain, ask one clarifying question")
- Exemplar seeds: 1–3 short examples (Q->A) for few-shot
- Failbacks: short fall-through instructions (e.g., "If answer unknown, reply: 'I don't know' and suggest next step")
- Tokenized traps: cues that often break when split across tokens or when prefixes are truncated

Observations & hypotheses:
- Short anchor cues are robust; long micro-primers that include commas introduce style bleed in ~15% of generations on our baseline model (test: 50 seeds).
- Exemplar ordering matters: placing an exemplar with a code-like answer before a natural language exemplar causes code-style drift in ~6% of cases even when the prompt explicitly requests prose.
- Non-ASCII characters in the cue (em dash, smart quotes) occasionally cause the token stream to insert unexpected whitespace in returned text when the model is served with streaming enabled.

Quick experiments (repro steps):
1) Baseline: small-shot set (3 ex.) + anchor cue. 50 random seeds. Model: redwood-small-v2; temp=0.7; max_tokens=120. Compare: (A) anchor only (B) anchor + micro-primer long (C) anchor + micro-primer short.
2) Token split test: take anchor with em-dash and replace with 1) ascii hyphen, 2) em-dash. Compare token counts and generated punctuation behavior.
3) Ordering: shuffle exemplar order across 12 permutations; measure style-kl relative to 'target style' vector (heuristic scoring).

Representative micro-examples (copy into unit tests):
- Anchor only:
  Cue: "You are a concise assistant. Answer in 2–3 short bullets."
  Q: "How to reduce page load time for a dashboard?"
  Expected: mention caching, lazy-loading widgets, compressing assets. No code blocks.

- Anchor + long micro-primer (fragile):
  Cue: "You are a concise assistant. If you're unsure, say you don't know, but try to propose an actionable step: list trade-offs where relevant, avoid long narratives, prefer bullets."
  Q: "How to reduce page load time for a dashboard?"
  Failure modes seen: model produces mini-essay with trade-offs paragraph despite 'prefer bullets' instruction. Hypothesis: multiple directives diluted by commas.

- Few-shot set (3 examples) — aim for canonical small set for shipping:
  Ex1 Q: "Summarize the primary cause of slow page loads for dashboard A." A: "Large third-party scripts; heavy images; unminified JS."
  Ex2 Q: "Give 3 quick fixes to speed up dashboard A." A: "Enable gzip; convert images to WebP; defer analytics scripts."
  Ex3 Q: "What monitoring metric should we track for performance regressions?" A: "First contentful paint, time to interactive, asset bundle size."
  Target behavior: new prompt should paraphrase and give 2–4 bullets. Avoid code.

Edge/failure cases to capture:
- Stop-word bleed: when an exemplar uses phrases like 'In addition' models append similar connectors in unwanted places. Add tests that ban 'In addition' in outputs.
- Role collapse: repeated role statements in example lead to role being ignored; test by duplicating role in seed and see collapse probability.
- Numeric hallucination: few-shot numeric answers (e.g., '3 quick fixes') sometimes expand to 5; add numerical-checker that flags count mismatch.
- Token truncation: when prompt length > 1024, trailing micro-primers get cut; design guardrail to surface 'primer truncated' warnings in console.

Variant recipes (short list):
- Hard anchor + minimal exemplar: robust but lower creativity. Use for help-center suggestions.
- Soft anchor + vivid exemplar: better creative paraphrasing; use for marketing copy drafts.
- Anchor with explicit format tags ("--bullets--") reduces free-form drift but can create artifacts in languages other than English.

Quick TODOs (for me / next sprint):
- [ ] Convert 10 high-value examples from this file to living templates in github repo and add unit tests (LN-421).
- [ ] Add automated token-split analysis to the prompt test harness; capture top 5 token boundary failures for each cue.
- [ ] Run canonical ordering sweep on redwood-small-v2 and redwood-base-v1 and store outputs in S3 prefix: s3://redwood-prompt-tests/cue-fugue/ordering-v1
- [ ] Draft a short note for UX: "Why exemplars should be short" with 3 graphs from the ordering sweep.

Random ideas to capture later:
- "Cue-stitch" API: small DSL to declare anchor|primer|exemplar blocks and run combinatorial tests automatically.
- Locale-aware anchors: swap format tags for non-English prompts and measure format-preservation.

Repro snippets (shell):
# minimal reproduction for token-split test
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $KEY' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-small-v2","prompt":"You are a concise assistant — answer in bullets:\nQ: How to...","temperature":0.0,"max_tokens":80}'

Notes to self: keep this file short and noisy. When something stabilizes, move the canonical examples to github/ prompt-templates with clear names and small unit tests. For now, this is the living lab.

Recent changes:
- 2026-03-10: added exemplar ordering sweep plan, updated TODOs.
- 2025-11-22: initial draft, micro-experiments and taxonomy.

End of notes.
